strengths: Well-motivated and practical problem: video object insertion with occlusion handling and illumination consistency is commercially relevant, and the paper clearly articulates the two core challenges (4D-aware placement and appearance-faithful generation).

The 4D-aware mask generation module (Uni4D-based reconstruction + scene-flow propagation + reprojection) is a sensible, well-engineered solution to propagating user-specified placement across frames, and the ablation (Fig. 5, Fig. 7, Table 3) shows each component contributes measurably, including occlusion integrity and object motion tracking on moving supports.

ROSE++ is a thoughtful dataset contribution: inverting the ROSE removal dataset into insertion triplets, with a VLM-based object retrieval step to avoid copy-and-paste artifacts. The comparison against random-frame crops (Table 2) directly validates this design choice.

The ablation study is unusually complete: quantitative Table 3 in the supplementary matches the qualitative Fig. 5 rows, and the illumination/shadow improvements from ROSE++ fine-tuning are demonstrated qualitatively (Fig. 6) as well as in VBench scores.

Evaluation covers quantitative metrics (CLIP-I, DINO-I, VBench), a user study with 20 participants and 6 criteria (Table 4), and extensive qualitative comparisons, consistently showing favorable results against Kling and Pika-Pro.
Clear writing and a well-structured presentation; implementation details (Wan2.1-VACE-14B, LoRA rank/iterations, resolution, training time) support reproducibility of the fine-tuning stage.
weaknesses: Limited comparison with research baselines: the related work cites GenProp, Invi, VideoAnyDoor, DreamInsert, etc., but the only quantitative comparisons are against commercial tools (Kling, Pika-Pro). Since VideoAnyDoor and GenProp claim strong VOI results, omitting them weakens the 'significantly outperforms existing research' claim in the abstract.

Comparison fairness is not fully controlled: commercial baselines are prompted textually and have no access to the reference image, mask, or 4D-aware placement used by the proposed method, so some of the gap (especially CLIP-I/DINO-I) may reflect conditioning differences rather than generative quality. This should be explicitly discussed.

Evaluation scale is small: VOIBench contains only 50 source videos / 100 generated outputs, crawled by the authors themselves, raising both statistical and potential selection-bias concerns; no other VOI benchmark is used.

Substantial component-level novelty concerns: the system is an assembly of existing models (Uni4D, SEA-RAFT, SAM2, TRELLIS-based single-view 3D, Wan2.1-VACE + LoRA). The generative model contribution reduces to LoRA fine-tuning on ROSE++, so the main novel assets are the pipeline design and the dataset; the paper would benefit from sharper justification of what is technically new versus integration.

Synthetic-to-real gap is not analyzed: training uses only the synthetic ROSE++ data, but evaluation is on real crawled videos. No quantitative analysis of generalization failure modes, nor an ablation on ROSE++ size/diversity.

Methodological limitations are underexplored: scene-flow propagation assumes approximately rigid local motion of the nearest K points and a single averaged translation per frame, which may fail for rotating or deformable interactions; the dependence on accurate Uni4D reconstruction (depth, camera pose) in low-texture or fast-motion scenes is not stress-tested; handling of multi-object interactions (apple/plate example) is only idealized.
Missing details hamper reproduction: the VLM used for ROSE++ is cited only as [1] (GPT-4 report) with unspecified values of n and m, and no statement about releasing code, data, or VOIBench.

Several writing issues remain (e.g., the incomplete sentence in Section 4.4 'we observe that information such as the position...', inconsistent Table numbering between main text and supplementary), and the paper lacks a limitations discussion.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem: video object insertion under real-world occlusions and lighting effects, with clear relevance to advertising and post-production.

The ROSE++ dataset construction is a genuinely useful idea: inverting an object-removal dataset into an insertion triplet and using VLM-based object retrieval (with DINO-based ranking) to obtain clean reference images. Table 2 provides evidence that this avoids copy-and-paste artifacts compared to random-frame crops.

The 4D-aware mask generation pipeline (reconstruction, user placement, scene-flow propagation, reprojection) is a sensible solution for occlusion-consistent mask propagation, and the ablation (Fig. 5, Table 3, Fig. 7) isolates its contribution reasonably well.

The evaluation includes ablations across all proposed components, a user study with per-criterion preferences, a clear retrieval prompt, and implementation details (model, LoRA rank, training schedule), which supports reproducibility of the core method.
weaknesses: Limited and weakly-matched baselines. The paper claims existing academic VOI methods (GenProp [14], VideoAnyDoor [25], INVI [21], Anything in Any Scene [2], DreamInsert [32]) fail under occlusion (Sec. 2), yet no quantitative or qualitative comparison against any of them is provided. The only baselines are two closed-source commercial tools (Pika-Pro, Kling), whose internal mechanisms differ entirely. This substantially weakens the central empirical claim that the framework 'significantly outperforms existing research and commercial models.'

The method is largely a composition of existing components (Uni4D [30] for 4D reconstruction, SEA-RAFT [26], TRELLIS [29], SAM2 [20], Wan2.1-VACE [9], LoRA, an off-the-shelf image inpainting model). The novel technical contribution is mainly the ROSE++ data recipe and pipeline design; no component is technically deep, and the paper does not articulate why this particular orchestration is a generalizable contribution rather than an engineering effort.

The evaluation benchmark (VOIBench) is small and self-collected: 50 crawled clips / 100 generated videos, with objects 'crawled' by the authors. Combined with training on a synthetic dataset and evaluating on the authors' own benchmark, there is a risk of distribution bias in favor of the proposed method. No external or public benchmark is used.

Several metrics are under-specified or questionable. 'Multi-View Consistency using VBench metrics' is never precisely defined as a computable quantity; CLIP-I/DINO-I restricted to masked regions do not measure occlusion correctness or background realism; and no perceptual quality metric or FVD-style statistic is reported. The quantitative margins over Kling on the VBench columns are small (e.g., Background Consistency 0.9429 vs. 0.9335; Imaging Quality 0.7101 vs. 0.7069), so headline claims rest heavily on the subject-consistency metrics and the user study.

The user study is small: 20 participants on ~10% of a 50-video test set (roughly 5 clips, 6 questions), yielding around 60 votes per criterion. The reported large preference margins (e.g., 79% vs. 19%) may be real, but statistical significance is not discussed and the sample is too small to support strong production-quality claims.

The 4D mask generation stage is validated only end-to-end. There is no quantitative evaluation of mask accuracy, 4D reconstruction quality, or failure analysis of the scene-flow propagation (Eq. 2, an averaged K-NN flow heuristic). Failure modes of the reconstruction stage on dynamic scenes, reflective surfaces, or fast motion are not discussed, and the paper has no limitations section.

A train/test domain gap exists: training uses synthetic ROSE renders while inference targets real crawled videos. The paper claims illumination transfer (Fig. 6) but does not quantify illumination/shadow fidelity with any metric; claims rest on qualitative examples.

Writing quality issues reduce clarity: incomplete sentences in the ablation discussion (Sec. 4.4, 'we observe that information such as the position of the person's arm and scarf... compared to the source video'), inconsistent figure/table references, and Fig. 2's architecture panel is difficult to parse. Table 1 in the main text and Table 3 in the supplement duplicate content, and the main-text quantitative section refers to 'Table 3' without a corresponding main-text table.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and underexplored task (video object insertion with user-specified placement, occlusion handling, and illumination consistency) with a clear two-stage design: 4D-aware mask generation followed by diffusion-based video synthesis.

The core technical ideas are sensible and well-motivated: using a 4D scene representation (Uni4D-style) to propagate a user placement into temporally coherent masks, scene-flow-based object propagation for physical interactions, and a first-frame inpainting anchor to transfer image-level insertion fidelity to video.

ROSE++ is a useful dataset contribution: cleverly inverting the ROSE object-removal data into insertion triplets, with a VLM-based reference-image retrieval step that avoids copy-and-paste train/inference discrepancies. The ablation (Table 2) directly supports this design choice.

Experimental evidence is multi-faceted: quantitative comparisons against commercial baselines (Table 1), a quantitative component-wise ablation (Table 3), a user study with six criteria (Table 4), and extensive qualitative comparisons including failure modes of baselines (supplementary Figs. 9-13).

The ablation study is informative: it isolates the contribution of the 4D-aware mask, first-frame inpainting, and ROSE++ fine-tuning, showing each addresses a distinct failure mode (occlusion preservation, subject identity, shadow/illumination synthesis).
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual components: the framework is largely assembled from existing pieces (Uni4D for 4D reconstruction, SEA-RAFT for flow, SAM2 for segmentation, TRELLIS-style single-view reconstruction, VACE with LoRA fine-tuning). The contribution is system integration and dataset curation rather than a new algorithmic idea; a stronger justification of why this specific integration is non-trivial would help.

No comparison against academic VOI/inpainting baselines that are cited as related work (e.g., VideoAnyDoor, Invi, GenProp, DreamInsert, VideoAnydoor). The only baselines are commercial text-driven tools (Kling, Pika-Pro), which take different inputs (text prompts rather than masks and reference images). This makes the claimed 'significantly outperforms' somewhat unfair and hard to situate against the actual state of the research field.

Both the training set (ROSE++, derived from synthetic ROSE data) and the evaluation set (VOIBench, crawled) raise generalization concerns. There is no analysis of the synthetic-to-real gap, no statistics on how often 4D reconstruction fails, and VOIBench (50 clips) is small; there is also no commitment to releasing VOIBench or ROSE++, which hurts reproducibility.

The method assumes a static inserted object rigidly attached to local scene flow; inserting moving or interactive objects is out of scope, and failure cases of the pipeline (e.g., reconstruction errors propagating to masks, mask artifacts visible in generation) are not discussed. The paper lacks a limitations section entirely.

The user study is small (20 participants, 10% of test videos) and its protocol/details (statistical significance, per-criterion variance) are thin. Additionally, there are minor inconsistencies in the manuscript (e.g., text refers to 'Table 3' where Table 1 appears; Kling slightly wins motion smoothness, which is not discussed).

No runtime/efficiency analysis despite the multi-stage pipeline (4D reconstruction, optical flow, VLM retrieval, 50-step diffusion at 832x480 over 81 frames), which matters for the claimed production-readiness.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-motivated framework that addresses two clearly identified gaps in Video Object Insertion: 4D-aware geometric placement and optics-aware synthesis that extends beyond object masks. The paper is well positioned relative to both mask-free and mask-conditioned VOI paradigms.

The Optics-Aware Representation Alignment is a clever and novel training strategy: using an extended (optics) mask as a stop-gradient teacher to force fine-mask conditioning to anticipate out-of-mask lighting effects. The attention-map analysis (Fig. 7) provides convincing mechanistic evidence that the aligned model externalizes activations beyond the object boundary, and the +7.3 dB optics-region PSNR gain with unedited-region fidelity preserved (33.30 vs 33.31) directly supports the claim.

ROSE++ is a valuable open contribution: reorganizing ROSE as (source, target, mask, reference) quadruplets and using editing-model-generated reference images with DINO-based rejection sampling is a sensible way to prevent copy-and-paste shortcuts. The control experiment against randomly-cropped references (Table 4 left) validates this design choice.

Fair-comparison methodology is above average: the paper supplies identical masks and edited first frames to baselines (e.g., VACE variants), and the Table 2 comparison (VACE fine-tuned on ROSE++ with 4D masks vs. bbox masks) credibly attributes gains to the proposed design rather than data exposure.

Extensive evidence: quantitative comparisons against commercial (Kling, Pika-Pro) and open-source baselines, progressive ablations isolating each component, paired LPIPS/PSNR/SSIM evaluation on held-out data, and two user studies (general and optics-focused) that both favor the proposed method.

Reasonable limitations discussion, implementation details (training cost, inference time, LoRA rank, mask post-processing) that support reproducibility, and clear writing with well-structured figures.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on existing components: Uni4D, SEA-RAFT, SAM 2, TRELLIS, VACE, and an image insertion model are orchestrated rather than substantially advanced. The primary algorithmic novelty is confined to the alignment loss, which is conceptually simple; a critic could argue the paper is closer to an applied/systems integration than a foundational contribution.

Sim-to-real gap for optical effects: ROSE++ is derived from simulator-rendered ROSE data, so the supervised lighting signals may not cover the diversity, spectral characteristics, and complexity of real-world illumination. The paper claims strong generalization but provides only indirect evidence (benchmark metrics and user studies) rather than a direct analysis of when/why the model fails on real lighting phenomena.

The evaluation relies heavily on training-tied metrics: CLIP-I/DINO-I and VBench-style scores can favor models that preserve the conditioning signal. LPIPS/PSNR/SSIM paired evaluation is only possible on the synthetic ROSE++ test split; on the real VOIBench there is no ground truth for inserted objects, so photometric realism claims rest partly on subjective user studies with modest participant counts (20 and 30).

Rigid-object and simple-propagation assumptions limit generality: the KNN scene-flow aggregation (Eqs. 2-4) assumes the object moves with nearby surfaces and cannot handle independent object motion, deformation, or contact changes; several pipeline choices (K, TopK, masking thresholds) are under-specified in the main text.

VOIBench (200 clips) is introduced but not released as a formal benchmark contribution with a defined protocol/leaderboard; its role relative to ROSE++ and to prior insertion benchmarks could be clarified, and single-frame anchor editing plus first-frame propagation means long videos with large viewpoint changes may accumulate drift, which is not quantified.

Some ablation deltas are small relative to the presentation: Config (c) vs. full model differs mainly in background consistency and imaging quality on VBench, and multi-view consistency improvement from ROSE++ references (0.5865 vs 0.5295) is reported without variance or significance analysis.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap in video object insertion: the tension between mask-conditioned control (background preservation) and the ability to synthesize optical effects (shadows, reflections) that extend beyond the mask boundary.

The evaluation is unusually careful for this area: the authors include a fair-comparison variant (VACE fine-tuned on ROSE++ with the same 4D mask, and with a coarse bbox mask) that disentangles the contribution of their optics-aware design from mere data exposure (Table 2), and a dataset-construction ablation against trivially cropped references (Table 4 left).

The ablation study (Table 3, Fig. 6) is progressive and isolates each component (4D mask, first-frame anchoring, LoRA fine-tuning, alignment loss), and the attention-map analysis (Fig. 7) provides mechanistic evidence that the alignment loss transfers external-activation behavior from the extended-mask teacher to the fine-mask student.

Two user studies (20 and 30 participants, including an optics-focused subset) complement automated metrics, and the optics-region PSNR analysis (+7.3 dB on optics mask, no degradation in unedited regions) directly supports the claim that L_align improves shadow rendering without harming background fidelity.
The ROSE++ dataset and VOIBench, if released as promised, are useful community resources for a task lacking supervised training data for optical effects.
Limitations are honestly stated (physics-aware interactions out of scope), and inference cost/engineering details (H200 training time, B200 inference memory) support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is modest. Each stage is largely an assembly of existing components: Uni4D for 4D reconstruction, TRELLIS for image-to-3D, SEA-RAFT for flow, SAM 2 for mask refinement, Wan2.1-VACE as the backbone, and an off-the-shelf image insertion model for first-frame anchoring. The core methodological contribution reduces to a simple KNN scene-flow displacement aggregation (Eq. 3-4) and a stop-gradient feature alignment loss (Eq. 7). The system-level integration is competent but the individual ideas are incremental.

The extended mask M_ext is derived from pixel-wise differences between paired source/target videos. This supervision is only available because ROSE++ reuses the ROSE removal benchmark, which is simulator-rendered; whether the alignment generalizes to real-world illumination physics (contact shadows on textured surfaces, reflections, inter-reflections) is claimed but only weakly demonstrated — the paired ground-truth evaluation (Table 4 right) is conducted on the held-out ROSE++ split, i.e., in the same synthetic domain as training, not on real videos.

Circularity concerns in evaluation: VOIBench is a self-introduced benchmark with crawled objects, and subject-consistency metrics (CLIP-I/DINO-I) combined with first-frame anchoring via an image insertion model may favor methods that tightly anchor to the reference image, potentially inflating identity scores relative to more generative baselines. VBench metrics are known to be noisy proxies for perceptual realism.

The scene-flow propagation assumes the inserted object is rigid and co-moves with its K-nearest scene points; plausible for objects resting on moving supports, but it offers no mechanism for objects in contact with multiple differently-moving surfaces, and no quantitative evaluation of mask-propagation accuracy is provided (only qualitative Fig. 9).

Some quantitative margins are small (e.g., ablation step from Config (c) to full model changes DINO-I from 0.5678 to 0.5669, i.e., slightly worse), and Motion Smoothness is below Kling; the paper's assertion that this is 'within VBench's per-clip noise' is not backed by any statistical test or variance estimate.

The paper does not discuss societal considerations relevant to a tool explicitly aimed at realistic object insertion into real footage (potential misuse for misinformation/deceptive content placement), which for a production-oriented editing framework deserves at least acknowledgment.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important gap in video object insertion (VOI): combining 4D-aware geometric placement with photometric realism (shadows/reflections), a combination that prior mask-free and mask-conditioned methods handle only partially.

The Optics-Aware Representation Alignment is a clever and technically sound idea: aligning fine-mask intermediate features to stop-gradient extended-mask features teaches the model to anticipate optical effects beyond the mask while requiring no extra input at inference. The attention-map analysis (Fig. 7) and paired optics-region PSNR (+7.3 dB) with unchanged unedited-region PSNR provide convincing evidence that the mechanism works as claimed.

Substantial dataset/benchmark contribution: ROSE++ (quadruplet dataset with reference images generated via a rejection-sampling pipeline that discourages copy-and-paste shortcuts, validated by the multi-view consistency ablation in Table 4-left) and VOIBench (200 clips spanning scene/occlusion/lighting axes).

Evaluation is notably thorough for this area: commercial (Kling, Pika-Pro) and open-source baselines, a fair VACE variant conditioned on the same masks, fine-tuned-VACE controls that isolate the contribution of the optics-aware design from mere data exposure, progressive ablations, and two user studies (including an optics-focused one on 50 shadow/reflection-rich clips).

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: training details (Wan2.1-VACE-14B, LoRA rank 128, 6500 iterations), inference cost measurements, extended-mask noise-cleaning details, and prompts are provided; ROSE++ and VOIBench are stated as open-sourced.

Limitations are honestly discussed (physics-aware interactions out of scope), and the failure-mode analysis of baselines in the supplementary is detailed and fair regarding differing input modalities.
weaknesses: The framework is largely an integration of existing components (Uni4D, TRELLIS, SEA-RAFT, SAM 2, VACE, LoRA, an image insertion model). The genuinely new technical elements are relatively simple (KNN scene-flow aggregation, the alignment loss with stop-gradient), so the novelty is more systems/engineering than algorithmic; the paper would benefit from framing this more explicitly as an Applied/Systems contribution.

The quantitative evidence for optics-aware rendering is computed only on the held-out ROSE++ (synthetic) split. The central claim of photorealistic optical effects on real-world videos is supported primarily by no-reference metrics (CLIP-I, VBench) and user studies, which are weaker proxies; no paired or geometry-aware quantitative evaluation of insertion placement accuracy on VOIBench is provided for the 4D mask propagation stage itself.

Some ablation deltas are small: in Table 3 the align-loss step barely moves CLIP-I/DINO-I and background consistency, and in Table 4-right Ours is slightly worse than Ours w/o L_align on object-mask LPIPS/PSNR. The narrative of strictly progressive improvement is stronger than the numbers in a few cells.

The extended mask is derived from source/target pixel differences, which is only feasible in supervised settings with ground-truth insertion; the synthetic-to-real generalization argument is asserted rather than quantified (e.g., no analysis of failure rates on VOIBench categories like low-light or initially-occluded scenes).

Baselines lacking mask/reference inputs (AnyV2V, ReVideo, Señorita) are evaluated in adapted settings, and commercial tools via text prompts; despite the authors' care, direct comparability remains imperfect, and no human evaluation of the mask propagation module in isolation is given.

No discussion of potential misuse (e.g., realistic object insertion in videos enabling misleading content) or dataset licensing/provenance for the crawled VOIBench clips, which would be expected for a production-oriented video editing system.

Presentation issues: several qualitative figures (Fig. 5, D4-D7) are dense and hard to parse at print scale; some terminology (e.g., 'object retrieval' in the supplementary prompt title vs. reference-image synthesis) is inconsistent.
